overview: Xixia, or Western Xia, was the Tangut imperial state in western China, conventionally dated 1038 to 1227. This imported map record instead runs from 1000 to 1279. Its broad, nearly repeated outlines are approximate and chronologically misleading: the early interval precedes the imperial proclamation, while the final interval extends well beyond Mongol conquest. It must not suggest that an independent Western Xia still existed in 1279.

periods.title: Before the imperial proclamation
periods.summary: The imported map begins earlier than the conventional 1038 starting date of imperial Western Xia.

periods.title: Independent Western Xia
periods.summary: The Tangut imperial state endured until Mongol conquest in 1227.

periods.title: The map label outlasts the state
periods.summary: This interval is imported coverage after conquest, not continued Xia independence.

sections.title: A state of trade, languages and skilled builders

items.text: Western Xia brought Tangut rulers and communities into a state also inhabited by Han Chinese, Tibetans, Uyghurs and other peoples. Its royal burial landscape lies beside the Helan Mountains in Ningxia. The tombs combine Chinese imperial planning with Buddhist forms and local choices, leaving evidence of a court that drew on several cultural traditions.

In eleventh-century diplomacy, Western Xia used its position on trade routes toward Central Asia to bargain with the Song court. Historian Jeongwon Hyun finds that benefits could arrive as official return gifts. A ceremonial exchange between rulers could therefore also be a commercial negotiation, with access to valuable goods at stake.

Builders at the imperial cemetery worked with rammed earth, brick and timber. They also created flood defenses: the surviving system includes 26 dikes and six drainage ditches. Protecting royal monuments meant thinking about moving water as well as impressive walls. These drains served the burial landscape; they are not evidence for toilets in ordinary houses.

Land-sale contracts from Khara Khoto describe farms by their canals, water supplies and neighboring plots. Households built homes on their own farmland, producing a scattered settlement pattern. In this dry region, canals brought water from the Black River to crops. A field’s value depended on more than its size: getting water to it mattered.

A grain-loan document from 1217 names the borrower’s wife as a co-borrower. Other surviving contracts also record wives sharing responsibility for repayment. Such papers bring a household into view: borrowing food could create obligations for more than one family member. Signing alongside a spouse had financial consequences.

An employment contract drawn up at the end of 1219 arranged nine months of work in the following year, from the first month to the tenth. Part of the payment was due immediately. The agreement covered the agricultural season from sowing through harvest. Advance payment and a written work schedule were already practical matters.

Khara Khoto’s surviving papers now help researchers recover names and activities that royal chronicles often overlook. The British Library’s Tangut collection includes material recovered during Aurel Stein’s 1913 to 1916 expedition. The site’s documents span the tenth to fourteenth centuries, so scholars must date individual pieces before assigning them to independent Western Xia.

sections.title: Learning, books and a few Tangut characters

items.text: In 1190, Gule Maocai compiled a Tangut-Chinese wordbook known as the Pearl in the Palm. It put two languages together for learners who needed to cross a linguistic boundary. The surviving book has 37 leaves. Its usefulness was very practical: knowing one language did not automatically make the neighboring language readable.

That wordbook also preserves the work of printers and bookbinders. Its butterfly binding folded sheets with their printed faces inward and attached their blank backs. Lotus decorations filled otherwise awkward spaces in the layout. Even a serious vocabulary book had room for a little visual flair, while its construction shaped how readers turned the leaves.

A late eleventh-century Da’an coin offers a tiny writing sample: “𘜶𗵐𘏨𘔭,” meaning “precious coin of the Da’an reign period.” This is a modern character transcription of its Tangut inscription, following Andrew West’s reading. On the coin, the four characters run clockwise from the top. The National Museum of China catalogues a Da’an example only 2.4 centimeters across.

Western Xia’s Buddhist printing needed organized craft work. Under royal patrons including Emperor Renzong and Empress Luo, institutions handled the production of sacred books; a character-carving bureau worked with Tangut texts. Surviving illustrated front pages let historians examine the people and techniques behind those books, beyond simply counting how many titles existed.

A major Buddhist gathering in 1189 at Dadumin Monastery combined the distribution of sacred texts with public acts of generosity. The account describes food for monks and poor people, the release of captive animals and pardons for prisoners. The ceremonies continued for ten days and nights. Religious patronage could involve meals and crowds as well as books.

A ritual banner found in Yinchuan’s Hongfo pagoda names Zhao Zhong and his family as donors. Their home was in neighboring Jin territory, in Zhenrong Prefecture. Dated between 1190 and 1227, the banner records a family’s religious connection across a political border. An object offered at a temple could carry the names of people living elsewhere.

Three Tangut medical prescriptions preserved in Russia concern sores on children’s heads. Modern researchers translated them and compared them with Chinese medical writings in a study published in 2016. These small texts document attention to children’s health and the exchange of medical knowledge. They preserve attempted treatments; the manuscripts alone cannot tell us whether those treatments helped.

Tangut writing continued after the kingdom’s conquest. At Mogao, a stele erected in 1348 commemorated Prince Sulaiman and his family’s support for a temple. Its Buddhist mantra appeared in six scripts, including Tangut. This later monument belongs to the Mongol era and shows why the end of a government is not automatically the end of its written culture.

ending.text: Mongol conquest ended independent Western Xia in 1227. The map’s 1279 endpoint is not a later fall date. Tangut texts and the 1348 Sulaiman stele show that language and religious traditions continued under changed political rule; conquest did not make the population or its culture disappear.
